title: 1 Kings 5:1–12
context: 1 Kings 5:1–12 records Solomon’s agreement with Hiram king of Tyre. In the Hebrew text these verses are numbered 5:15–26; the WEB follows the English numbering. Hiram, who had loved David, sends envoys, and Solomon explains that David could not build a house for the LORD’s name because of wars, but the LORD has now given rest, so Solomon will build as the LORD promised David (2 Samuel 7:12–13). Hiram blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son and agrees to supply cedar and cypress in exchange for food for his household. The section closes by noting that the LORD gave Solomon wisdom as promised and that the two kings made a treaty. Arminian and Reformed readers share the reading that God’s promise to David is now being carried out through peace, wisdom, and ordinary cooperation, even with a foreign king.

verses.text: Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon, for he had heard that they had anointed him king in the place of his father, and Hiram had always loved David.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram king of Tyre sends servants to Solomon after hearing of his anointing, because Hiram had always loved David. Arminian readers see the friendship between Hiram and David, a foreign king, continuing into the next generation and opening the way for cooperation in building the LORD’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence using international relationships to accomplish his promise to David. Both traditions note Hiram’s earlier help with David’s house (2 Samuel 5:11) and read the verse as setting the stage for the temple.

verses.arminianNotes: Solomon sends a message to Hiram. Arminians see Solomon taking initiative in the work God had promised, acting wisely through diplomacy rather than waiting passively, and they read the short verse as introducing his speech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the speech that follows grounds the project in God’s promise to David. Both traditions read the verse as a simple narrative transition that introduces Solomon’s explanation of his plans.

verses.text: “You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the wars which were around him on every side, until the LORD put his enemies under the soles of his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon explains that David could not build a house for the LORD’s name because of the wars around him until the LORD subdued his enemies. Arminian readers see God’s timing in the work, since the temple waits for a time of rest that God himself provides.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that 1 Chronicles 22:8 adds that David had shed much blood. Both traditions read the verse as stressing that the temple belongs to God’s plan and timing, and that the "name" of the LORD represents his revealed presence.

verses.text: But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is no enemy and no evil occurrence.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon says the LORD has given him rest on every side, with no enemy or misfortune. Arminians see rest as God’s gift that brings opportunity and responsibility, since Solomon must now use the peace for God’s purposes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and connect the rest with the promise of Deuteronomy 12:10–11, which links rest in the land with the place God would choose for his name. Both traditions see God’s faithfulness fulfilling his word to Israel.

verses.text: Behold, I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD spoke to David my father, saying, ‘Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place shall build the house for my name.’
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon intends to build a house for the LORD’s name, as the LORD told David that his son would build it. Arminian readers see Solomon acting in faithful response to God’s word, receiving the promise as a task to carry out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that Solomon quotes the promise of 2 Samuel 7:12–13, so the temple is the fulfillment of God’s own word. Both traditions see the promise and Solomon’s obedience working together in the project.

verses.text: Now therefore command that cedar trees be cut for me out of Lebanon. My servants will be with your servants; and I will give you wages for your servants according to all that you say. For you know that there is nobody among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.”
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks Hiram to have cedar cut in Lebanon, offering wages for his servants and acknowledging that the Sidonians are the best at cutting timber. Arminians see Solomon’s wisdom in recognizing others’ skill and paying fairly for it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see God’s gifts of skill given even to those outside Israel and used for his house. Both traditions read the verse as showing that ordinary labor and trade can serve God’s purposes.

verses.text: When Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly, and said, “Blessed is the LORD today, who has given to David a wise son to rule over this great people.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram rejoices and blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son to rule a great people. Arminian readers note that a foreign king speaks in praise of Israel’s God, which shows the LORD’s reputation spreading through Solomon’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that blessing a nation’s god in diplomatic speech was a customary courtesy, so the verse does not tell us whether Hiram personally believed. Both traditions read it as confirming that Solomon’s wisdom came from the LORD.

verses.text: Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, “I have heard the message which you have sent to me. I will do all your desire concerning timber of cedar, and concerning cypress timber.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram agrees to all Solomon’s wishes concerning cedar and cypress timber. Arminians see a willing partnership in which both kings freely agree to terms, and they see God’s purposes advancing through human cooperation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see God’s providence providing the materials needed for his house. Both traditions read the verse as part of a diplomatic exchange that shows the peace God had given Solomon.

verses.text: My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea. I will make them into rafts to go by sea to the place that you specify to me, and will cause them to be broken up there, and you will receive them. You will accomplish my desire, in giving food for my household.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram’s servants will bring the timber to the sea, float it in rafts to the place Solomon names, and break it up there, while Solomon supplies food for Hiram’s household. Arminian readers see a fair exchange that benefits both sides.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the practical details of transport by sea. Both traditions read the arrangement as an example of how the temple was built through ordinary commerce, which God used for his purposes.

verses.text: So Hiram gave Solomon cedar timber and cypress timber according to all his desire.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram gives Solomon all the cedar and cypress timber he wants. Arminians see Hiram keeping his word, and they see the abundance of materials as a sign of God’s blessing on the project.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the verse as fulfilling the agreement exactly. Both traditions read it as showing God’s provision for his house through the willing help of a foreign king.

verses.text: Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat for food to his household, and twenty cors of pure oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon gives Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of pure oil each year. The WEB footnotes give these as about 120,000 bushels and about 1,100 gallons. Arminian readers see Solomon paying generously and keeping his side of the agreement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 2:10 lists different quantities and goods, which interpreters explain in different ways. Both traditions read the verse as showing the scale of the work and Solomon’s faithfulness to his agreement.

verses.text: The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty together.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD gave Solomon wisdom as he promised, and there was peace with Hiram and a treaty between them. Arminians see God’s promise in 1 Kings 3:12 being kept, and they see Solomon’s wise use of that gift in making peace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the narrator credits Solomon’s wisdom to the LORD. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s gift producing peace and fruitful relationships, with Solomon at his best in this period.
